paras: The attempted lynching of Elijah Church took place on a Sunday night in September 1881, when a crowd of about fifty people entered the jail at Taylorsville, Alexander County, North Carolina, intending to hang Church, who was accused of murdering Miss Caroline Thompson during a robbery. The crowd gave up after R. Z. Linney urged it to let the law take its course. Church was then moved to the jail at Newton for safety, and in early October a mob took him from that jail and hanged him.

Miss Caroline Thompson was killed in Alexander County during a robbery at the house of 'old man Thompson'; the Charlotte Democrat placed the killing 'some months ago', while later wire reports said it happened the previous August. Harrison Dockery, held in the Taylorsville jail, confessed and named Elijah, or 'Lige', Church of Wilkes County as his partner. According to Dockery, Church struck Miss Thompson with an axe after she recognized him, and the two men then shared the money with John Adams of the Brushy Mountains, who was arrested and released on $500 bail.

Dockery's arrest followed a letter from a postmaster in Alleghany asking whether a murder had been committed in Alexander, since two men calling themselves Dockery and Church were spending money freely there.

Church was captured on Lewis' Fork in Wilkes on September 9 by Eller and Minton, the latter his brother-in-law, and brought to Taylorsville the next day. The Charlotte Democrat said his brothers-in-law handed him over for the reward and expected him to escape, and the Lenoir Topic reported a general opinion that the capture was a 'put up' job. He was found carrying a dirk, a file and a bottle of 'acqua fortis', which were taken from him, and the jail was guarded at night 'to prevent either rescue or lynching.'

On the Sunday night after the capture, a crowd of fifty 'invaded the jail with the purpose of hanging the prisoner.' In the Lenoir Topic's account, the crowd changed its mind only after Linney made 'an impassioned speech to let the law take its course.' No injuries were reported, and no member of the crowd was named.

At Church's preliminary hearing, the only evidence was Dockery's sworn testimony that the two men had gone into a regular business of 'robbery and plundering.' The Topic said feeling in Alexander was 'very strong' and traced the urge to lynch to fear that a trial would drag on, drain the county's finances and end in acquittal 'upon a technicality.' To guard against a renewed attempt, Church was moved to the Catawba County jail at Newton.

Wire reports from Wilmington dated October 7 said a mob had taken Church from the Newton jail and hanged him, and the Charlotte Home and Democrat described him as 'a white man.' Sheriff Mays of Alexander County then took Dockery to the Charlotte jail for safety, and that paper suggested that friends of the other men Dockery's testimony might implicate had lynched Church.

The Taylorsville attempt reached print through the Lenoir Topic, whose account the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic reprinted on September 22 under the heading 'The Alexander Murder' and whose longer version the Charlotte Democrat carried on September 30 as 'The Thompson Murderers.' These reports called Church and Dockery 'scoundrels' and Church 'notorious', gave Dockery's confession as the story of the crime, and described the crowd at the jail without editorial comment.

The later hanging at Newton travelled further, as short wire paragraphs headed 'Necktie Social in North Carolina' in Wheeling and 'Mob Law in North Carolina' in Savannah. The Farmer and Mechanic, following the Wilmington Star, wrote that Church's lynching was 'to be regretted', since there was no reason to think he would not have been tried and convicted.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Elijah Church
bases: A crowd of fifty entered the Taylorsville jail 'with the purpose of hanging the prisoner' and was turned back by a speech, so this is an attempted lynching (A2, A3, A4).

At Taylorsville no one was killed: a crowd of 50 meant to hang Church, who was accused of murder, but gave up after Linney's speech (A2); he was hanged by a mob at Newton about three weeks later, and that is a separate episode (A5, A11).
Both accounts of the jail attempt are reprints of the Lenoir Topic, one in the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic and one in the Charlotte Democrat (A2, A3, A4); no independent report was found.

accounts.label: Lenoir Topic (as reprinted)
accounts.gist: A crowd of 50 invaded the Taylorsville jail on Sunday night to hang Church and gave up only after Linney urged them to let the law take its course; the Topic blamed fear of a slow, costly trial ending in acquittal.

accounts.label: Dockery's confession and testimony
accounts.gist: Dockery said that he and Church robbed the Thompson house and that Church killed Miss Thompson with an axe after she recognized him.

framing.detail: Under 'The Alexander Murder' and 'The Thompson Murderers', the Lenoir Topic reprints told the jail attempt as a news item, without praise or blame, and credited Linney with turning the crowd away.
After the later Newton hanging, the Farmer and Mechanic, quoting the Star, said the lynching 'is to be regretted' because Church would have been convicted anyway.
The Newton hanging ran in wire paragraphs headed 'Necktie Social in North Carolina' and 'Mob Law in North Carolina'.
